newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian Congress votes to bankrupt drug lords.
newsitem.headline: Colombian Congress votes to bankrupt drug lords.

text.p: In an abrupt about-face, Colombia's Congress overwhelmingly approved on Thursday the retroactive seizure of property and assets accumulated by the country's billionaire drug barons over the past 20 years.

The lower house of Congress, which rejected the measure just 48 hours earlier, passed it by a huge 103-4 majority after intense lobbying by government officials and business leaders in favour of a bill that could help stave off possible U.S. economic sanctions next year.

U.S. officials have warned that sanctions were a virtual certainty unless Colombia adopted stiff new penalities for drug traffickers, including a so-called asset forfeiture law allowing the authorities to confiscate their vast real estate holdings and other property.

The sweeping bill drafted by the government in July -- and approved in its entirety by the Senate last week -- would allow the government to seize hundreds of million dollars in drug-related property accumulated in Colombia over the past two decades.

But the House watered it down in a highly controversial vote on Tuesday night, ruling instead that property linked to convicted drug lords would only be liable to forfeiture if it were accumulated in the aftermath of Colombia's 1991 constitution.

Government officials led by President Ernesto Samper rejected the House vote as a national disgrace and a new vote -- by both the Senate and House -- was called late on Thursday after a congressional conference committee agreed to throw out the earlier results and try again.

In the new vote, the Senate moved to approve the bill unanimously. In the House, the government left no question about its knack for arm-twisting and Colombia-style politicking by winning over 44 votes in just two days.
"This constitutes one of the country's greatest achievements," Samper said in a triumphant statement moments after the House vote, which cleared the way for his signing the bill into law.
"Congress has demonstrated its sense of responsibility to the country," added Sen. Claudia Blum, a vocal supporter of anti-drug legislation.

Blum, a native of the southwest city of Cali, took exile in Miami last month because of death threats against her and her family. She returned only recently to particpate in what she and others described as an historic opportunity to prove Colombia's commitment to the global anti-drug fight.
"I think Congress has vindicated itself with Colombians and with the international community," Blum said.

Estimates vary as to how much money could be confiscated by the state under the law Samper is now expected to sign within the next few days. But some drug kingpins, including the jailed leaders of the Cali cartel, are said to have amassed personal fortunes totalling up to $12 billion.

According to government estimates, traffickers own or wield effective control over up to 25 percent of Colombia's farm land. Much of that property is to be cut up into small parcels and turned over to landless peasants under terms of the asset forfeiture law.
